content: Inspectors should closely observe the premises to identify signs of rodent infestation. They should specifically look for active rodent pathways or burrows in the yard, entry points into buildings, burrows under walls or along ditch banks, evidence of rodent damage, fresh fecal droppings near foundations, and other indicators of infestation. It is beneficial to have a supervisor or another field inspector recheck the survey findings on a subsequent day to verify the results. For example, a 10% sample of the surveyed premises can be re-inspected to confirm the accuracy and completeness of the recorded information. In some cases, householders may refuse to grant permission for Integrated Pest Management (IPM) staff to inspect their premises or dwellings. Such refusals should be documented on the report form and referred to the supervisor. In other instances, no responsible adult may be present to provide permission for inspection. In these situations, the IPM authority's policy will determine whether an exterior inspection should be conducted. The term interior inspection generally refers to the main buildings on a premises and does not typically include sheds or outbuildings, although this can be adjusted based on the needs of the local IPM authority. It is recommended that interior inspections be conducted by two-person teams, as the work is detail-oriented, tedious, and often challenging due to clutter, furniture, and crowded conditions. Inspectors should examine all rooms in the building for signs of rodent activity and sanitation deficiencies. Particular attention should be given to kitchens, closets, bathrooms, attics, and basements, as these areas are especially attractive to commensal rodents. All floor levels of the building should be inspected, regardless of the suspected rodent species. Norway rats are typically found in basements and lower floors, roof rats are more likely to inhabit upper floors and attic spaces, and house mice can be found almost anywhere, including in cabinet drawers and above drop ceilings. Householders can often provide valuable information about a rodent infestation. In some communities, managing or controlling the interior rodent population may be more challenging than addressing the exterior population. The exterior inspection form can be modified for interior inspections to include details such as level/floor, room type, number of occupants, and evidence of active rodent signs (e.g., droppings, holes, gnawed materials, and rub marks). Information about rodent bites should also be collected. Infestation rates, defined as the percentage of apartments in a building with active rodent signs, are useful for comparing conditions or measuring IPM progress over time. Inspection teams should adhere to standardized procedures for interior inspections. For example, in a multifamily apartment building, the inspection should begin in the basement and proceed upward, inspecting apartments in numerical order, followed by the attic or crawlspace, and finally the roof (if accessible). Each apartment should be entered through the main door, and the wall containing the main door, as well as everything on or touching that wall, should be inspected for signs of rodents and potential entry points. The inspection should then proceed clockwise to the next wall, continuing until all walls have been inspected. Next, the floor area, including anything on or touching the floor, should be inspected, followed by the ceiling area, including anything on or touching the ceiling. Each room should be inspected in the same manner, and closets should be inspected in association with specific walls of a room. This standardized inspection method provides precise data on rodent locations, which is essential for targeted intervention. The data also facilitate tracking specific changes over time and provide valuable information for other inspectors. The Block Record Exterior Rodent Inspection and Sanitation Form is used to document information on rodent infestation and environmental deficiencies for each premises on a block. The form includes space for recording information for up to 10 premises, with additional forms used as necessary. Inspectors should enter the page number in the designated space at the top right corner of the form (e.g., 1 of 2, 2 of 2). If only one form is required for a block, the notation 1 of 1 should be used to clarify that only one page is needed. Inspectors' names should be entered at the top of the form in the designated space, and other items at the top of the form should be completed by the supervisor or team leader before the teams enter the field. The location of a block should be indicated by writing the names of the streets that form the block in the block diagram space in the upper left portion of the form. A copy of the assignment chart should be kept in the inspector's or supervisor's office. Completed inspection forms should be reviewed and initialed by the inspectors. All columns of block data should be totaled and recorded on the appropriate line of the summary form. The summary form should be used to prepare progress reports, identify problems, and allocate resources effectively. As inspectors proceed clockwise around a block, they should write each street address in the left column of the form. If an indoor inspection has been conducted at a particular address, the line number (1 to 10) in the No. column should be circled. Premises must be classified into one of four categories: residential, commercial and residential, commercial, or vacant lot. Only one of the first four columns should be checked. For residential premises, a check should be placed in the corresponding column if the unit is a home or dwelling (defined as an enclosed space used for living purposes). A dwelling can be a single-family or multifamily unit. The number of dwelling units should be entered in the designated column. For premises used for both commercial and residential purposes, a check should be placed in the appropriate column. For premises used solely for commercial purposes (including parking lots) or other nonresidential purposes such as offices, churches, clubhouses, or schools, a check should be placed in the commercial column. The type of premises (e.g., school) may also be written in the address column. Some IPM programs may use a code for recording public properties, clubs, churches, or other types of nonresidential properties. For vacant lots, a check should be placed in the corresponding column if the lot has no structure on it. Note that a parking lot should be designated as commercial.
